title: Emily Post: Ettiquette Queen
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro voice, Chuck) profile Emily Post, the American socialite, novelist and etiquette writer. They cover her wealthy Baltimore/New York upbringing, her father architect Bruce Price and Tuxedo Park, her unhappy marriage to Edwin Post and his blackmail-driven exposure of affairs, her novels and magazine articles, her 1922-era etiquette book (619 pages, bestseller), its philosophy of ethics and "good society" over mere wealth, its characters and the Mrs. Newwood disastrous dinner party example, her later revisions, the pen-name parody "How to Behave Though a Debutante," the 1927 death of son Bruce the Deuce, her architecture book, her syndicated column, and the Emily Post Institute's modern advice on grief. The episode closes with a listener mail correction about pronouncing Sault Ste. Marie.
topics: How to Behave Though a Debutante

segments.title: Opening banter on Emily Post
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode and express admiration for Emily Post and her etiquette book.

segments.title: Emily Post's approach to etiquette and ethics
segments.summary: Discussion of how Post's etiquette book emphasized ethics and good society rather than wealth, and how it challenged the aristocratic-style etiquette books of the time in a society of equals.

segments.title: Childhood, family and Tuxedo Park
segments.summary: Post was born Emily Price in 1872 to architect Bruce Price and heiress Josephine Lee Price. The family moved to New York, and Bruce Price built cottages in Tuxedo Park, the enclave where the tuxedo originated.

segments.title: Marriage to Edwin Post and family
segments.summary: Post married Edwin Post after a debutante ball, had two sons, Ned and Bruce, and the marriage was unhappy; her father died in 1903 and encouraged her writing.

segments.title: Novels, blackmail scandal and divorce
segments.summary: Post wrote novels including The Flight of the Moth. Edwin's affairs and his decision to expose blackmailers brought shame, and they divorced the next year.

segments.title: Post's writing career and road trip
segments.summary: After the divorce Post wrote more novels and magazine articles. She went on a 45-day cross-country trip with son Ned along the Lincoln Highway, which led to the book By Motor to the Golden Gate.
topics: By Motor to the Golden Gate

segments.title: Writing the 1920 etiquette book
segments.summary: Post's etiquette book deal in 1920 came after World War I and the Spanish flu; her sons doubted the timing. The 619-page Etiquette became a bestseller. Jane McGrath's article was the basis of the episode.

segments.title: Contents, characters and the etiquette philosophy
segments.summary: The book covers conversation, invitations, thank-you notes, and household matters, presented in narratives with characters like the Worldlies, Kindhearts and Toplofties. Post frames good society around manners, charm and consideration for others.

segments.title: Mrs. Newwood's disastrous dinner party
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the excerpt where Mrs. Newwood's extravagant dinner party goes badly, and the lessons about being kind to people below one's station and to younger generations.

segments.title: Later novels and the death of Bruce Post
segments.summary: Parade was her last novel. In 1927 her son Bruce died of a ruptured appendix after refusing to go to the hospital, and Post threw herself into work.

segments.title: Revisions, parody book and public fame
segments.summary: Post revised her etiquette book about ten times, updating advice on chaperoning and dating. She published the racy parody How to Behave Though a Debutante under the pen name Muriel, then revealed herself. She also wrote The Personality of a House, had a syndicated column, and was ranked second only to Eleanor Roosevelt by Pageant Magazine.
topics: How to Behave Though a Debutante

segments.title: Emily Post Institute and grief etiquette
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Emily Post Institute's modern guidance, including what not to say to grieving people and how to offer specific help, and close with a quote on likableness.
topics: what not to say to grieving people

segments.title: Listener mail: Sault Ste. Marie pronunciation
segments.summary: A listener named Terrence Ward jokingly corrects the hosts' pronunciation of Sault Ste. Marie as a Canadian-themed joke.
